questions.question: How do you use verify() in Mockito to check method interactions?
questions.title: Mockito verify() Method | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: verify(mock).method(args) asserts that method(args) was called exactly once on the mock. If not called, or called with different args, the test fails. This is behavior verification — checking that your code interacted with dependencies correctly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's core interaction verification mechanism and when to use behavior verification versus state verification
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verify() to check return values instead of assertions on the actual result — verify checks that a method was called, not what it returned
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between state verification (assertions on results) and behavior verification (verify on interactions), and give a concrete scenario where behavior verification is essential

sections.title: Understanding verify() — Behavior Verification in Mockito
sections.content:
**verify()** is Mockito's core mechanism for **behavior verification** — checking that your code called a dependency's method with the right arguments. Unlike **state verification** where you assert on return values, verify() focuses on interactions.

Think of it like a security camera: you're not checking what the person bought, you're checking that they walked through the door at all. This matters when the method has **side effects** — like saving to a database, sending an email, or logging an event — where there's no return value to assert on. By default, verify(mock).method() checks that the method was called **exactly once**. If the method wasn't called, or was called with different arguments, the test fails immediately with a clear error message showing what was expected versus what actually happened.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|verify()|~Assert a call happened|verify mock method|checks the interaction|after the action
blue|Times Control|~How many calls|times n|never and atLeast|atMost
emerald|With Matchers|~Match arguments|eq and any|all-or-none rule|the argument captor

sections.title: Verifying Method Calls on a Mock Repository
When to Use verify()
sections.content:
Use **verify()** when testing methods with **side effects** — operations that change state outside the method itself. For example, when your service calls repository.save() to persist an entity, there's no return value to assert on, but you need to confirm the save happened.

Use it to check **logging** calls: verify(logger).warn() to ensure warnings were logged for specific error conditions.

Use it for **notification systems**: verify(emailService).send() to confirm emails were triggered. Also use verify() when testing **exception handling**: verify that cleanup methods like transaction.rollback() or connection.close() were called when an exception occurred. The key pattern: if the method's purpose is to trigger an action rather than compute a result, verify() is your tool.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with verify()
sections.content:
- **Verifying return values**: Freshers often write verify(mock).getValue() and then try to assert on what it returned — but verify() doesn't return the method's result, it just checks the call happened. Use when().thenReturn() to stub the return value, then assert on the result your code produces.
- **Over-verification**: Adding verify() for every single mock interaction makes tests brittle. Only verify interactions that are **critical** to the behavior you're testing. If your service calls getUserById() to get data but the important part is what it does with that data, don't verify the getUserById() call.
- **Wrong argument matchers**: Using verify(mock).method(any()) when you actually care about specific arguments. If the exact value matters, pass it directly: verify(mock).method(expectedValue).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **verify(mock).method()**: asserts the method was called exactly once with those exact arguments
- **Behavior verification**: checking that interactions happened, not checking return values or results
- **Side effects**: verify() is essential for void methods like save(), delete(), send() where there's no result to assert on
- **Default count**: verify() without a count assumes times(1) — the method was called exactly once
- **Argument matching**: you can verify with exact values or matchers like any(), eq(), or custom matchers
- **Failure feedback**: when verification fails, Mockito shows what was expected and what actually happened
- **Not for stubbing**: verify() checks calls that already happened, it doesn't control what the mock returns

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say verify is how you check that your code called a method on a mock with the right arguments. It's behavior verification — you're asserting that an interaction happened, not checking what it returned. So if I've got a service that calls orderRepository dot save, I write verify orderRepository dot save order to make sure that call actually occurred. This matters a lot for void methods or methods with side effects, like saving to a database or sending an email. There's no return value to assert on, so verify is how you confirm the action took place. By default, verify checks the method was called exactly once. If it wasn't called at all, or was called with different arguments, the test fails. One thing freshers mess up is trying to use verify to check return values. That's not what it does. You stub the return value with when then-return, then you assert on the result your code produces. Verify just checks the call happened. I also wouldn't verify every single mock interaction — only the ones that are critical to the behavior being tested. Over-verifying makes tests brittle because they break whenever implementation details change, even if the behavior is still correct.

questions.question: What is ArgumentCaptor in Mockito and how do you use it?
questions.title: Mockito ArgumentCaptor | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: ArgumentCaptor captures the argument that was passed to a mock method so you can assert on it. Use it when the argument is constructed inside the method under test and you can't compare it directly — like a dynamically created object passed to save().

interviewer_intent.testing: Advanced Mockito usage for capturing and inspecting method arguments, especially common in Spring service layer tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using eq() or any() when you actually need to inspect the argument contents — ArgumentCaptor gives you the real object to assert on
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the full pattern: @Captor annotation or ArgumentCaptor.forClass(), verify with capture(), then getValue() to extract and assert on the captured object's fields

sections.title: What ArgumentCaptor Does — Capturing Arguments for Inspection
sections.content:
**ArgumentCaptor** is a Mockito tool that **captures** the actual argument passed to a mock method during the test so you can **inspect** it afterward.

Think of it like a net that catches the object as it flies into the mock, then hands it back to you for examination. This is crucial when the argument is **created inside** the method under test — you don't have a reference to it, so you can't compare it directly. For example, if your service creates a new User object, sets fields dynamically, and passes it to userRepository.save(), you need ArgumentCaptor to grab that User and verify its fields were set correctly. Without ArgumentCaptor, you'd have to use **any(User.class)** which just checks the type, not the content. ArgumentCaptor closes this gap by giving you the exact object that was passed, letting you assert on individual fields like username, email, or role.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|ArgumentCaptor|~Grab passed arguments|capture in verify|inspect afterwards|assert on fields
blue|How It Works|~Two steps|forClass(Type)|capture inside verify|getValue to read
emerald|When to Use|~Complex objects|built inside the method|no getter exposed|assert deep state

sections.title: Capturing and Asserting on a Dynamically Created Entity
When to Use ArgumentCaptor
sections.content:
Use **ArgumentCaptor** when the argument to a mock method is **created inside** the method under test and you need to verify its fields. Common scenario: a service method that constructs a new entity, populates it, and saves it — you want to check the entity was built correctly.

Use it for **DTO transformation**: when your controller converts a request DTO to an entity, capture the entity to verify all fields mapped properly.

Use it for **event publishing**: if your service creates an OrderCreatedEvent and publishes it, capture the event to assert on the event payload. Also useful for **batch operations**: if your code calls saveAll with a list of entities, use ArgumentCaptor forClass List dot class to capture the entire list and assert on its size and contents. The pattern: when you can't directly reference the object being passed because it's created internally, ArgumentCaptor is the bridge to inspect it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with ArgumentCaptor
sections.content:
- **Using any() when you need inspection**: Freshers often write verify repository dot save any User dot class when they actually need to check field values. That just verifies the type, not the content. Use ArgumentCaptor to capture and inspect the actual object.
- **Forgetting getValue()**: After calling capture, you must call getValue to extract the captured argument before asserting on it. Freshers sometimes try to assert directly on the captor itself.
- **Multiple captures**: If the method was called multiple times, getValue returns the last captured value. Use getAllValues to get a list of all captured arguments.
- **Overuse in simple cases**: If you're just verifying an exact object you already have a reference to, pass it directly to verify — don't use a captor. Use verify mock dot method expectedObject, not capture then compare.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ArgumentCaptor**: captures the argument passed to a mock so you can assert on it afterward
- **Declaration**: use at-Captor annotation or ArgumentCaptor dot forClass Type dot class
- **Capture**: pass captor dot capture as the argument in verify statement
- **Extract**: call captor dot getValue to get the captured object for assertions
- **Multiple calls**: use captor dot getAllValues to get a list of all captured arguments if the method was called multiple times
- **Field assertions**: once captured, you can assert on individual fields like savedUser dot getEmail
- **Not for stubbing**: ArgumentCaptor is only for verification in verify statements, not for stubbing in when-thenReturn

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ArgumentCaptor is how you grab the actual argument that was passed to a mock so you can inspect it. It's really useful when the argument is created inside the method you're testing, so you don't have a direct reference to it. For example, if my service creates a new User object, sets the username and email, and then calls userRepository dot save, I can't just pass that User to verify because I never had a variable for it. That's where ArgumentCaptor comes in. I declare it with the at-Captor annotation, then in my verify statement I pass captor dot capture as the argument. After that, I call captor dot getValue to extract the actual User that was passed, and now I can assert on its fields like username and email to make sure they were set correctly. The common mistake is using any User dot class when you actually need to check the content. That just verifies the type, not the values inside. ArgumentCaptor gives you the real object to inspect. If the method was called multiple times, you'd use getAllValues instead of getValue to get a list of all the captured arguments. It's a super common pattern in service layer tests where you're verifying that entities or DTOs were constructed properly before being saved or sent somewhere.

questions.question: What is verifyNoMoreInteractions() and when should you use it?
questions.title: Mockito verifyNoMoreInteractions | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock) fails if any method was called that wasn't already verified. Use it to ensure a mock wasn't called unexpectedly. However, overuse makes tests brittle — prefer verify(mock, never()).specificMethod() for targeted negative assertions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding of when to use comprehensive versus targeted verification, and awareness of test brittleness trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding verifyNoMoreInteractions on every mock in every test, making tests overly strict and brittle to refactoring
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the trade-off between comprehensive verification and test maintainability, and give a specific scenario where strict verification is actually valuable

sections.title: Understanding verifyNoMoreInteractions — Strict Interaction Checking
sections.content:
**verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock)** is Mockito's strictest verification mode — it fails the test if **any** method was called on the mock that you didn't explicitly verify with a verify() statement.

Think of it like an audit trail: after you've checked off all the interactions you expected, this ensures there are no **surprise** calls lurking. The intent is to catch **unintended side effects** — if your refactored code accidentally started calling an extra method, this would catch it. However, it's a double-edged sword. Overuse makes tests **brittle** because they fail whenever the implementation changes, even if the change is harmless. For example, if your service starts calling logger.debug() for diagnostics, every test with verifyNoMoreInteractions will break. The recommendation: use it **sparingly** in high-stakes scenarios like payment processing or security operations where you genuinely need to ensure no unexpected interactions occur, but avoid it in normal business logic tests where implementation flexibility matters.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|verifyNoMoreInteractions|~Nothing else happened|after your verifies|catches stray calls|a strict guarantee
blue|The Risk|~Brittle tests|breaks on refactor|couples to calls|use sparingly
emerald|Often Better|~Targeted verifies|verify each call|never for negatives|clearer intent

sections.title: Code Example
Step 1 — Assess the Risk of Unverified Calls
sections.content:
First, determine whether unverified interactions on this mock pose a **real risk**. Ask: what happens if this mock's methods are called unexpectedly? For a **payment gateway** mock, an extra charge() call could double-bill a customer — that's a real risk, so strict verification makes sense.

For a **logger** or **metrics** mock, extra calls are benign — they don't change business outcomes, so verifyNoMoreInteractions adds no value. For a **repository** mock in a read operation test, an unexpected save() call would be concerning — but you can target that specific risk with verify(repo, never()).save(any()) instead of blanket verifyNoMoreInteractions. The decision: if the mock controls **external systems**, **money**, or **security**, consider strict verification. If it's internal infrastructure like logging or caching, skip it.

sections.title: Step 2 — Weigh Test Brittleness Against Safety
sections.content:
Second, evaluate the **maintenance cost** of strict verification. Tests with verifyNoMoreInteractions fail whenever the implementation adds a new interaction, even if it's intentional and correct. For example, if you add a notification step to your order flow, every test with verifyNoMoreInteractions(orderRepository, emailService) will break and need updating.

This creates **friction** in refactoring — developers avoid improving code because it breaks too many tests. The trade-off: strict verification gives you confidence that nothing unexpected happened, but it **couples tests to implementation details**. Prefer **targeted negative verification** — verify(mock, never()).riskyMethod() — which checks the specific interaction you're worried about without locking down every other call. Use verifyNoMoreInteractions only when the risk of an unverified call outweighs the cost of brittle tests.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with verifyNoMoreInteractions
sections.content:
- **Blanket usage**: Freshers add verifyNoMoreInteractions to every test because they think it makes tests "more thorough". In reality, it makes them fragile — tests break when implementation details change, not when behavior changes. Only use it for specific high-risk mocks.
- **Confusing with verifyNoInteractions**: verifyNoInteractions(mock) checks that no methods were called at all; verifyNoMoreInteractions checks that no additional methods beyond what you already verified were called. They're different tools.
- **Not considering test intent**: If your test is checking that an order was saved, you don't need to verify that the cache wasn't updated or the logger wasn't called. Focus verification on the behavior being tested, not every possible side effect.
- **Ignoring alternatives**: Instead of verifyNoMoreInteractions(paymentGateway), you can write verify(paymentGateway, never()).refund(any()) to specifically check that refund wasn't called, which is more precise and less brittle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **verifyNoMoreInteractions**: fails if any method on the mock was called that wasn't covered by a verify statement
- **Audit mode**: ensures no surprise interactions occurred beyond what you explicitly checked
- **Brittleness trade-off**: makes tests strict but fragile — they fail when implementation changes even if behavior is correct
- **Targeted alternative**: prefer verify(mock, never()).specificMethod() to check specific risks without locking down all interactions
- **Use case**: valuable for high-stakes mocks like payment gateways or security services where unexpected calls have real consequences
- **Avoid for infrastructure**: don't use on loggers, metrics, or caching mocks where extra calls are harmless
- **Not the same as verifyNoInteractions**: that checks zero calls; this checks zero additional calls after verify statements

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: verifyNoMoreInteractions is Mockito's strictest verification — it fails the test if any method was called on the mock that you didn't already verify. It's like an audit: after you've checked off all the interactions you expected, this makes sure there aren't any surprise calls you missed. The idea is to catch unintended side effects, like if your refactored code accidentally started calling an extra method. But here's the trade-off — it makes tests really brittle. If your implementation changes and adds a new interaction, even a harmless one like a debug log, every test with verifyNoMoreInteractions breaks. So the recommendation is to use it sparingly, only in high-stakes scenarios. For example, with a payment gateway mock, you'd want to ensure no unexpected charge calls happened, because that could double-bill a customer. But for a logger or a cache, extra calls don't matter, so strict verification just creates maintenance headaches. A better approach for most cases is targeted negative verification. Instead of verifyNoMoreInteractions on the whole mock, you write verify mock comma never dot specificRiskyMethod to check the one thing you're worried about without locking down every other interaction. That way your tests stay focused on behavior, not implementation details.

questions.question: How do you verify that a method was never called in Mockito?
questions.title: Verifying a Method Was Never Called
questions.direct_answer: Use verify(mock, never()).method() to assert a method was never invoked, or verifyNoInteractions(mock) to assert no methods on the mock were called at all.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the VerificationMode options beyond the default times(1) and understand negative verification
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not verifying negative cases — assuming the absence of a call when you should explicitly assert it, especially for risky operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between never(), times(0), verifyNoInteractions(), and verifyNoMoreInteractions() and explain when each is appropriate with concrete examples

sections.title: Negative Verification — Asserting Methods Were Not Called
sections.content:
**Negative verification** in Mockito asserts that a method was **not** called, which is just as important as verifying positive interactions. Use **verify(mock, never()).method()** to check that a specific method with specific arguments was never invoked during the test. This is critical for **safety checks** — ensuring that risky operations like delete(), charge(), or sendEmail() didn't happen when they shouldn't.

Think of it like a circuit breaker test: you're not just checking that the safe path works, you're checking that the dangerous path is **blocked**. For example, if an order is invalid, you want to verify that paymentGateway.charge() was never called, not just that the validation failed. Mockito also provides **verifyNoInteractions(mock)** which is broader — it asserts that **no methods** on the mock were called at all. Use this when the entire mock should be untouched, like verifying that a notification service wasn't invoked in a dry-run mode. Both are essential for complete test coverage because they catch unintended side effects.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|never()|~Zero invocations|verify mock never|a negative assertion|guards side effects
blue|The Family|~Same goal|times zero|verifyNoInteractions|verifyNoMoreInteractions
emerald|Typical Tests|~Error paths|no save on invalid|no email on failure|no external call

sections.title: Verifying Risky Operations Were Not Called
When to Use Negative Verification
sections.content:
Use **verify(mock, never())** for **risky operations** where an unintended call has serious consequences. For **payment systems**, verify that charge() or refund() wasn't called when validation fails or in dry-run scenarios. For **data deletion**, verify that repository.delete() wasn't called when a user lacks permission or when the entity is marked as protected. For **notification systems**, verify that emailService.send() or smsService.send() wasn't triggered when the user has notifications disabled. For **audit logging**, verify that sensitive operations weren't logged when privacy mode is enabled.

Use **verifyNoInteractions(mock)** for mocks that should be **completely untouched** in certain scenarios — like a production payment gateway in a test environment, or a notification service in a background batch job that shouldn't send real emails. The pattern: if the absence of a call is part of the correct behavior, explicitly verify it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Negative Verification
sections.content:
- **Not verifying negative cases**: Freshers focus on happy path verification — checking that methods were called — but skip verifying that unsafe methods were not called in error cases. For example, testing that validation fails but not verifying that save() wasn't called afterward.
- **Confusing never() and times(0)**: They're equivalent — verify mock comma never dot method and verify mock comma times 0 dot method do the same thing — but never is clearer intent.
- **Using verifyNoInteractions when you mean never**: verifyNoInteractions checks that the entire mock was untouched. If you only care that one specific method wasn't called, use verify mock comma never dot specificMethod.
- **Forgetting argument matchers**: verify mock comma never dot delete userOne only checks that delete with that exact user wasn't called. If you want to ensure delete wasn't called with any argument, use verify mock comma never dot delete any.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **verify(mock, never()).method()**: asserts that method was never called during the test
- **verifyNoInteractions(mock)**: asserts that no methods at all were called on the mock
- **times(0)**: equivalent to never — both verify zero invocations, but never is more readable
- **Use for safety**: verify risky operations like delete, charge, send were not called in error paths
- **Argument matching**: use any() to verify the method wasn't called with any arguments, or specific values to check exact arguments
- **Test completeness**: negative verification is as important as positive — it catches unintended side effects
- **verifyNoMoreInteractions**: different from verifyNoInteractions — it checks for additional calls beyond verified ones

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To verify a method was never called, I use verify mock comma never dot method. This is negative verification — asserting that something didn't happen. It's just as important as verifying positive interactions because it catches unintended side effects. For example, if an order fails validation, I want to make sure paymentGateway dot charge was never called, not just that the validation error was returned. The verify mock comma never form checks that the specific method with those specific arguments wasn't invoked. If I want to ensure the method wasn't called with any arguments, I'd use verify mock comma never dot method any. There's also verifyNoInteractions mock, which is broader — it asserts that no methods at all were called on the mock. I'd use that when the entire mock should be untouched, like a notification service in dry-run mode. A common mistake freshers make is not verifying negative cases. They test the happy path and check that methods were called, but they don't check that unsafe methods weren't called in error paths. For risky operations like delete or charge or send, you should explicitly verify they didn't happen when they shouldn't, because assuming the absence of a call isn't enough.

questions.question: What is the difference between verify(mock, times(n)), atLeast(n), and atMost(n) in Mockito?
questions.title: Verify Invocation Count Modes
questions.direct_answer: times(n) asserts exactly n calls; atLeast(n) asserts at least n calls; atMost(n) asserts no more than n calls — all are passed as the second argument to verify().

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Mockito's VerificationMode API and when to use flexible versus strict call count assertions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verify(mock) without a count argument and assuming it checks for exactly one call — which is correct, but candidates often don't know the default is times(1)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that over-specifying call counts makes tests brittle and suggest only verifying counts when the count itself is business-critical, like ensuring retry logic doesn't exceed a limit

sections.title: Understanding VerificationMode — Controlling Call Count Assertions
sections.content:
**VerificationMode** is Mockito's API for specifying **how many times** a method should have been called. The default verify(mock).method() implicitly uses **times(1)** — the method was called exactly once. But Mockito provides flexible options: **times(n)** for exact counts, **atLeast(n)** for minimum bounds, **atMost(n)** for maximum bounds, and **never()** (equivalent to times(0)) for zero calls. These are passed as the second argument: verify(mock, times(3)).method().

Think of it like setting **acceptance criteria** for invocation counts. For example, if your service retries on failure, you might verify atMost(3) to ensure it doesn't retry indefinitely. If it processes a batch of items, you'd use times(batchSize). However, over-specifying call counts makes tests **brittle** — if you refactor to call a method twice instead of once for better separation, tests break even though behavior is correct. The recommendation: only verify counts when the count itself is **semantically important**, not just an implementation detail.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|times(n)|~Exact count|verify times two|fails on mismatch|the default is one
blue|atLeast / atMost|~Range checks|atLeast one|atMost three|flexible bounds
emerald|never()|~Zero calls|equals times zero|negative path|guards behaviour

sections.title: Code Example
sections.content:
```java
service.retrySend(message);

verify(sender, times(3)).send(message);   // exactly 3 calls
verify(sender, atLeast(1)).send(message); // 1 or more
verify(sender, atMost(5)).send(message);  // up to 5
verify(logger, never()).error(any());     // zero calls
```

sections.title: Comparison of VerificationMode Options
sections.content:
| Mode | Assertion | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| times(n) | Exactly n calls | Verify batch size or explicit count requirement |
| atLeast(n) | At least n calls | Retry logic must attempt minimum times |
| atMost(n) | No more than n calls | Retry logic must not exceed max attempts |
| never() | Zero calls (times 0) | Risky operation should not be invoked |
| default (no arg) | Exactly one call (times 1) | Standard single-call verification |

sections.title: When to Use Each VerificationMode
sections.content:
Use **times(n)** when the **exact count** is part of the specification. For example, if your batch processor must call saveAll() once per batch, verify times(1). If it processes 5 items and calls save() on each, verify times(5).

Use **atLeast(n)** for **retry logic** where you need a minimum number of attempts — like verifying that a failing API call was retried at least 3 times before giving up.

Use **atMost(n)** to enforce **upper bounds** — like ensuring retry logic doesn't exceed 5 attempts to avoid infinite loops or excessive costs.

Use **never()** for **safety checks** — verifying that delete() or charge() wasn't called in error paths.

Use the **default** (no count argument) for standard cases where you expect the method to be called once. The pattern: if the count has **business meaning** (batch size, retry limit), verify it; if it's just an implementation detail, don't lock it down.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with VerificationMode
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the default**: Freshers use verify(mock).method() without realizing it implicitly checks times(1). If the method was called twice, the test fails. They're confused why the test breaks even though the method was called.
- **Over-specifying counts**: Adding explicit times(1) or times(n) to every verify makes tests brittle. If you refactor and the call count changes (like splitting one call into two for clarity), tests break even though behavior is correct. Only verify counts when the count is **semantically important**.
- **Using times(0) instead of never**: They're equivalent, but never() is clearer intent.
- **Wrong mode for the need**: Using times(n) when you mean atMost(n) — for example, verifying retry logic with times(3) fails if it succeeded on the second attempt, but atMost(3) would pass. Choose the mode that matches your acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **VerificationMode**: second argument to verify that specifies how many times the method should have been called
- **times(n)**: asserts exactly n invocations — fails if more or fewer
- **atLeast(n)**: asserts at least n invocations — allows more, fails if fewer
- **atMost(n)**: asserts no more than n invocations — allows fewer, fails if more
- **never()**: equivalent to times(0) — asserts zero invocations
- **Default**: verify(mock).method() implicitly uses times(1) — exactly one call
- **Brittleness**: only verify counts when the count has business meaning, not for implementation details

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: VerificationMode is how you specify how many times a method should have been called in Mockito. The most common is times n, which asserts exactly n calls. For example, verify mock comma times 3 dot method checks that method was called exactly three times. If it was called more or fewer, the test fails. Then there's atLeast n, which asserts at least n calls — useful for retry logic where you want to ensure it tried at least three times before giving up. And atMost n, which asserts no more than n calls — useful for capping retry attempts to avoid infinite loops. There's also never, which is equivalent to times 0 — it asserts the method was never called at all. One thing freshers don't always realize is that the default verify mock dot method without a count argument is actually times 1 — it checks for exactly one call. If the method was called twice, the test fails. A common mistake is over-specifying call counts in every test. If you write times 1 explicitly everywhere, your tests become brittle — if you refactor and split one call into two for clarity, all those tests break even though the behavior is still correct. I'd only verify counts when the count itself is semantically important, like batch size or retry limits. If it's just an implementation detail, don't lock it down.
